lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- What Happened Last Night
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Veridiana Sterman Petrilli | Lesson 4 -- What Happened Last Night
lesson.grammar_point: past simple and past continuous with when, while and as soon as

listenings.text: People think a hotel overbooks by accident. It does not. We sell more rooms than we have because on a normal night four or five guests never turn up, and an empty room earns nothing. Nine nights out of ten the arithmetic works and nobody notices. On the tenth night everybody turns up, and I am the one standing at that desk. Here is what I was taught on my first shift, and I still do it. I tell the guest the truth in the first sentence, before they ask, because the anger comes from not knowing. Then I say what I am going to do, not what I cannot do. We pay for the room in the other hotel, we pay for the taxi, and we bring the guest back the next morning at no cost. And I have learned one more thing in eleven years. The guests who make a big noise do not get more than the guests who stay calm and ask a clear question. They only get it later, because while they are shouting, nobody is typing.

So this happened to me in Lisbon two years ago, and I still tell the story. We landed at eleven at night, it was raining, and when we got to the hotel there was a line of about nine people at the desk. Nobody was moving. While we were waiting, I heard the man in front of us shouting at the receptionist about a booking he had made in March. He shouted for ten minutes and he got nothing. When it was our turn, my wife did something very simple. She put the reservation on the counter, she smiled, and she asked one question: what can you do for us tonight? The receptionist typed for about forty seconds, and then she gave us a room in a better hotel two streets away, a taxi and breakfast. As soon as we walked out, the man was still at the desk, still shouting. It turned out he stayed there another hour.

reading.rtitle: The Night Nobody Had a Room
paras: The flight landed at eleven at night and it was raining. When Marta and her sister got to the hotel, four other people were already standing at the desk, and nobody was moving. They waited in the line for twenty minutes. The woman on duty kept saying the same sentence to everybody, in the same tone, and it was not the sentence anybody wanted to hear.

The hotel was overbooked. It was not a mix-up and it was not anybody's fault at the desk: the hotel sells more rooms than it has, because on a normal night some guests never arrive. That night everybody arrived. The man in front of Marta was making a fuss about a booking he had paid for in March, and while he was shouting, the woman behind the desk was typing and saying nothing.

When it was Marta's turn, she did something her sister still talks about. She put the confirmation on the counter, she said good evening, and she asked one question: what can you do for us tonight? The night manager stopped typing. She said the hotel would pay for a room in another hotel three streets away, a taxi in both directions, and breakfast, and she gave them a voucher for the taxi. It took four minutes.

As soon as they walked out, the man was still at the desk, still explaining March. Eventually he got the same room, the same taxi and the same breakfast, an hour and ten minutes later. It turns out that the desk had already sorted out four families that night, and every one of them got exactly the same thing. The difference was not the volume. The difference was the question.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from what night managers describe as a normal overbooked evening.

choices: To warn travellers never to book a hotel that overbooks rooms.
To show what actually happens on an overbooked night, and why one question worked better than ten minutes of shouting.
To explain how hotels calculate how many rooms to sell.

items: The hotel was overbooked because somebody at the desk made a mistake.
The text says it was not a mix-up and not anybody's fault at the desk: the hotel sells more rooms than it has, on purpose.
Marta and her sister were the first people at the desk.
Four other people were already standing there when they arrived, and they waited in the line for twenty minutes.
The man in front of Marta got less than she did.
He got the same room, the same taxi and the same breakfast, but an hour and ten minutes later.
The hotel paid for the taxi in both directions.
The night manager said the hotel would pay for a taxi in both directions, and she gave them a voucher for it.
Marta's whole conversation at the desk was short.
The text says it took four minutes.

items.situation: Say what the weather was doing when you arrived, in one sentence with two verbs.
tips: It was raining when we arrived.
The long action takes was + -ing; the short one takes the simple past.

items.situation: Say what other people were doing at the desk while you were waiting.
tips: While we were waiting, four other people were standing at the desk.
While almost always goes with the -ing form.

items.situation: Say what happened the moment the manager saw your confirmation.
tips: As soon as she saw our confirmation, she gave us a voucher.
As soon as = the second one thing ended, the next one started. Two simple pasts.

items.situation: Tell the end of the story with eventually.
tips: Eventually he got the same room, an hour later.
Eventually goes before the verb, or at the start of the sentence.

items.situation: Tell a real story of your own: something that went wrong on a trip, in three sentences with when or while.
tips: We were driving to the airport when the car stopped.
Keep the long action in was/were + -ing and the interruption in the simple past.

items.situation: Now say what you did about it, and how it ended.
tips: We called a taxi, and eventually we got there forty minutes before the flight.
Reason and result still apply: use because, so or that is why.
